paras: The Florence lynching threat was a demand by citizens of Florence, South Carolina, in late July 1900 that two Black prisoners charged with rape be returned to them from the state penitentiary in Columbia, a demand that state officials and a Columbia church paper read as the prelude to a lynching. Governor McSweeney refused, and the principal accused died in the penitentiary of wounds two days later. McSweeney cited the case in his re-election campaign as a lynching he had prevented, and a wire item printed in Wisconsin said he had called out the militia against a mob at the Florence jail.

About July 23, 1900, two Black men from Florence charged with rape were brought to Columbia "for safe keeping" and lodged in the penitentiary. The coverage names neither the accused nor the alleged victim and gives no account of the alleged crime. The Baptist Courier credited the sheriff of Florence County, together with the governor and "other officials and citizens," with protecting the prisoners.

On July 24, according to the Southern Christian Advocate's weekly news summary, Florence citizens held a mass meeting and asked the governor to return the prisoners to Florence, and he declined. The Baptist Courier wrote that there was "every reason to believe a lynching awaited the prisoners" had they been sent back, though it allowed that "possibly there was no danger." It added that the law-abiding people of Florence did not want a lynching and that the demand came from "certain citizens."
On July 26 the principal accused died in the penitentiary "from his wounds." The coverage does not say how or when he was wounded.

In a speech at York, reported on August 1, McSweeney said he had refused the "demand of the Florence people" to return to their sheriff "a Negro rapist" then held in the penitentiary. He promised to send troops to the trial and guard the jail until the day of execution if the man were convicted, a pledge the Yorkville Enquirer recorded as drawing cheers. In a campaign statement printed later in August, he said that because newspapers had kept him posted on "the state of feeling at Florence," a crime that would have been "a foul blot" on the state had been averted, and he used the case to defend his newspaper subscriptions. No report of a trial of the surviving prisoner was found.

All of the coverage found appeared in white papers, and no Black-press report of the episode turned up. In South Carolina the case reached print mainly through religious weeklies and campaign reporting. The Southern Christian Advocate listed the removal, the mass meeting and the death as bare items in its news summary, without comment. The Baptist Courier, by contrast, gave it an editorial, commending the officers who protected "the Negroes arrested and held for trial for a heinous crime" and wishing that such a course were followed more often so that the state "would not be disgraced by lynchings and mob violence."

The Yorkville Enquirer and the Fairfield News and Herald carried the episode only inside McSweeney's campaign speeches, where it served as proof of his stand against "mob law or lynch law." In both, the governor's account named the prisoner by the charge, as "a Negro rapist," or spoke only of "the prisoners." Outside the state the case appeared as a single wire sentence in the Wausau Pilot on August 14 and the Eagle River Review on August 16, some three weeks after the events.

The wire item says that "the mob refused to disperse" and that the governor "called out the militia to guard the jail." The South Carolina reports, closer to the events, describe instead a mass meeting and a request to the governor, with the prisoners already in Columbia, and mention troops only as something McSweeney would send to a future trial. The number held also differs: the Advocate and the wire item speak of two men, while McSweeney, in a speech reported after the principal accused's death, spoke of one man in the penitentiary.

reader.title: Florence lynching threat (1900)
bases: Citizens demanded two prisoners charged with rape in a way officials read as a lynching threat, and a wire item reports a mob at the jail (A2, A3, A4).
Every account describes a lynching that was prevented (A1, A3, A4, A6); the principal accused died of wounds in the penitentiary, but no paper attributes the wounds to a mob (A2).
South Carolina papers agree on the demand and the governor's refusal (A1, A2, A3), but the wire item's mob at the jail and militia guard are not supported by them (A4).

accounts.label: South Carolina news summary
accounts.gist: Two prisoners charged with rape brought to Columbia; Florence mass meeting asked for their return; governor declined; principal accused died of wounds.

accounts.label: Baptist Courier editorial
accounts.gist: Officers rightly refused to send the prisoners back, as a lynching likely awaited them, though possibly there was no danger.

accounts.label: Governor McSweeney's campaign speeches
accounts.gist: He refused the Florence people's demand for 'a Negro rapist' and, kept informed by newspapers, prevented a lynching.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: The governor tried to prevent the lynching of two Black men at Florence and called out the militia when the mob refused to disperse.

framing.detail: The Southern Christian Advocate listed the events as unadorned news-summary items.
The Baptist Courier editorial praised officers for protecting the prisoners and deplored lynchings and mob violence, while calling the charge 'a heinous crime'.
The Yorkville Enquirer reported the governor vowing to keep the prisoner to the law while calling him 'a Negro rapist', to cheers.
The Fairfield News and Herald printed McSweeney's statement that a lynching would have been 'a foul blot' on the state.
Wisconsin papers ran one wire sentence on the governor calling out the militia.

versions.value: Mob refused to disperse; militia called out to guard the jail
Mass meeting asked the governor to return prisoners already moved to Columbia; troops mentioned only for a future trial

conflicts.note: The South Carolina reports are nearer the events and more detailed; the wire item appeared three weeks later and may conflate the governor's promise of troops with what happened.
A1 was published after A2 reports the principal accused's death on July 26, which may account for the difference.

Two unnamed Black men charged with rape
Threat (demand for the prisoners); a siege appears only in the wire item and is contested
'Florence citizens' at a mass meeting; a 'mob' in the wire item
Moved from Florence to the state penitentiary in Columbia; not taken
The principal accused died of wounds in the penitentiary, cause unstated; no mob killing reported
